disclaimer: Informational only. Not a diagnosis, not a prediction of an individual reaction, and not a guarantee that a product is safe.
precautionary_pattern: may contain|traces? of|(manufactured|processed|made|produced) in a facility

milk.name: Milk / Dairy
milk.basics: Milk allergy is an immune reaction to milk proteins, not to lactose sugar (that is intolerance).
milk.science: Casein is heat-stable, so baking rarely removes it. Whey proteins are more heat-sensitive.
milk.cross_reacts_with: Goat and sheep milk; beef in a few people

peanut.name: Peanut / Groundnut
peanut.protein: Storage proteins Ara h 1, Ara h 2, Ara h 3
peanut.basics: Peanut is a legume, not a true nut. Its storage proteins survive cooking and digestion.
peanut.science: Ara h 2 is a major allergen linked to more severe reactions in many studies.
peanut.cross_reacts_with: Tree nuts (separate allergy, often co-occurs); lupin in some people

tree.name: Tree nuts
tree.protein: 2S albumins and vicilins (e.g. Ana o 3 in cashew)
tree.basics: Tree nut allergy involves storage proteins that are similar across several nuts.
tree.science: Cashew and pistachio share closely related proteins, so reacting to one can mean both.
tree.cross_reacts_with: Cashew ↔ pistachio; walnut ↔ pecan; others vary by person

egg.name: Egg
egg.basics: Most egg allergens are in the white. Ovomucoid is heat-stable, so cooked egg can still trigger reactions.
egg.science: "Albumin" or "lysozyme" on a label can be egg-derived. Check the source.

wheat.name: Wheat / Gluten
wheat.protein: Gliadins, glutenins and other wheat proteins
wheat.basics: Wheat allergy is an IgE reaction to wheat proteins. It differs from coeliac disease, an autoimmune condition triggered by gluten.
wheat.science: Barley and rye are listed because gluten-related proteins are shared (relevant mainly to coeliac disease).
wheat.cross_reacts_with: Barley, rye; grass pollen in some people

soy.name: Soy
soy.basics: Soy proteins are widely used as additives, so soy can appear in unexpected foods.
soy.science: Highly refined soy oil has little protein, but soy lecithin and soy flour contain more.
soy.cross_reacts_with: Other legumes, including peanut, in some people

fish.name: Fish
fish.basics: Parvalbumin is found in many fish species and is stable to cooking.
fish.science: Parvalbumins are structurally similar across fish, so many people react to several species.
fish.cross_reacts_with: Many other fish species; not usually shellfish

shell.name: Shellfish
shell.basics: Tropomyosin is the best-known shellfish allergen and is heat-stable.
shell.science: Tropomyosin is similar across crustaceans, molluscs and house-dust mites, which explains broad cross-reactivity.
shell.cross_reacts_with: Other crustaceans; sometimes molluscs; house-dust mite

sesame.name: Sesame
sesame.basics: Sesame appears in breads, snacks, chutneys, hummus and spice blends.
sesame.science: Sesame storage proteins are related to those of other seeds and nuts.
sesame.cross_reacts_with: Other seeds and some tree nuts in a few people

peanut.title: Ara h 2 (peanut)
peanut.note: Often described as a major peanut allergen. Verify ID before final use.

milk.title: Bos d 5 (beta-lactoglobulin)
milk.note: Major whey protein in cow milk.

shell.title: Pen a 1 (shrimp tropomyosin)
shell.note: Conservation across species is why cross-reactivity is discussed. Verify ID before final use.

sample_label: Wheat flour (maida), sugar, palm oil, milk solids, soy lecithin, cashew paste, salt, natural flavour. May contain peanuts and sesame.
